title: If You Were a Dad in 1960, This Was Your Life

scenes.text: If you were a father in nineteen sixty, you were probably in your thirties. You had served in the Second World War or Korea. You had come home, married your sweetheart, found a steady job and bought a house. Now you had two, three or four kids, a mortgage, a car payment, and a whole family depending on you. And you probably never once complained about it.
scenes.caption: A DAD IN 1960

scenes.text: Fathers of nineteen sixty are often remembered as quiet, serious men. Men in hats and overcoats, carrying a briefcase or a lunch pail. Men who didn't say much, but who showed up every single day. Many of us didn't really understand our fathers until we became parents ourselves.
scenes.caption: QUIET, SERIOUS MEN

scenes.text: So let's spend a week as a dad in nineteen sixty. From Monday morning at work to Sunday afternoon in the backyard. If your father was one of these men, I think you'll see him in almost every scene.
scenes.caption: ONE WEEK

scenes.text: The alarm clock rang at six. A wind-up clock with two bells on top, loud enough to wake the whole house. Dad shaved at the bathroom sink with a safety razor and a brush of shaving cream. A splash of Old Spice or Aqua Velva. Brylcreem in his hair. Then he put on a white shirt, a tie and a suit, or work clothes and steel-toed boots.
scenes.caption: SIX A.M.

scenes.text: Breakfast was eggs, bacon, toast and black coffee, made by his wife. He read the morning newspaper at the kitchen table, folded into quarters. He smoked a cigarette. The kids came down in their pajamas, and he gave each of them a quick pat on the head on his way out the door.
scenes.caption: COFFEE AND THE PAPER

scenes.text: Then off to work. In the suburbs, he might drive to the train station and ride the commuter train into the city. In a factory town, he walked or carpooled to the plant. On a farm, he'd already been working for two hours. Either way, he usually carried his lunch. A sandwich in wax paper, an apple and a thermos of coffee.
scenes.caption: OFF TO WORK

scenes.text: In nineteen sixty, a man often worked for the same company for his whole career. Thirty or forty years at the same plant, the same office or the same railroad. Loyalty went both ways. The company promised steady work and a pension, and the man promised to show up every day.
scenes.caption: ONE COMPANY FOR LIFE

scenes.text: Office men worked at metal desks, surrounded by typewriters, adding machines and filing cabinets. Secretaries took dictation in shorthand. Meetings were full of cigarette smoke. A three-martini lunch was not unusual for executives. And the men all wore the same thing. A gray flannel suit, a narrow tie and a fedora.
scenes.caption: THE GRAY FLANNEL SUIT

scenes.text: Factory men worked eight-hour shifts, often with overtime on Saturdays. The work was loud, hot and physical. Steel mills, auto plants, rubber factories, coal mines. A union job paid well, often enough to support a family of six. But many men came home exhausted, with sore backs and ringing ears.
scenes.caption: A UNION JOB

scenes.text: Many men worked a second job, too. A few nights a week at a gas station, driving a delivery truck on weekends, or doing carpentry for the neighbors. Farmers often worked at a factory in the winter. Teachers painted houses in the summer. The extra money paid for braces, piano lessons or a family vacation at the lake.
scenes.caption: A SECOND JOB

scenes.text: What did dad earn? In nineteen sixty, a man working full time earned about fifty-four hundred dollars a year, on average. That was enough for a house, a car, food, clothes and a little left over for a vacation. In most families, his paycheck was the only one, and everyone knew it.
scenes.caption: ABOUT $5,400 A YEAR

scenes.text: At five-thirty or six, Dad came home. In many houses, this was a ritual. The kids ran to the door. Mom had dinner almost ready. Dad hung up his hat and coat, loosened his tie, and sat down in his chair. Maybe he had a cocktail, or a cold beer. Maybe he just wanted ten minutes of quiet with the evening paper.
scenes.query: 1950s father coming home children running door
scenes.caption: FIVE-THIRTY

scenes.text: Then dinner. The whole family sat down together at the table. Dad sat at the head. Meat, potatoes and a vegetable. He might ask each child about school. Manners were expected. Elbows off the table. Napkin in your lap. And nobody left the table until they were excused.
scenes.caption: THE HEAD OF THE TABLE

scenes.text: Discipline was often Dad's job. Wait until your father gets home was a phrase that struck fear into millions of children. Fathers in nineteen sixty were usually stricter than fathers today. Spankings were common. But many of those same fathers would also do anything for their kids.
scenes.caption: WAIT UNTIL YOUR FATHER GETS HOME

scenes.text: Dad also handled the money. He paid the bills at the kitchen table once a month, writing checks and licking stamps. He balanced the checkbook with a pencil. He gave Mom an allowance for groceries and household expenses. And when a big purchase came up, like a new refrigerator, the family waited until Dad decided they could afford it.
scenes.caption: HE HANDLED THE MONEY

scenes.text: After dinner, Dad might watch television with the family. Gunsmoke, Perry Mason, The Twilight Zone, or a ball game. He controlled the channel, which meant getting up and turning a dial. He might fall asleep in his chair halfway through, and wake up just long enough to say he wasn't sleeping.
scenes.caption: HE WASN'T SLEEPING

scenes.text: Or he might be in the basement or the garage, working on a project. Building a bookshelf. Fixing a lamp. Tinkering with the car. Many fathers of nineteen sixty could fix almost anything. They kept coffee cans full of screws and nails, sorted by size. Children learned the names of tools by handing them over.
scenes.caption: HE COULD FIX ANYTHING

scenes.text: Some nights, he had a meeting. The Elks, the Moose, the Lions Club, the American Legion or the VFW. The church council. The school board. The bowling league on Wednesday nights. Fathers in nineteen sixty belonged to things. It was how they made friends and how they gave back to their town.
scenes.caption: THE BOWLING LEAGUE

scenes.text: Before bed, Dad made his rounds. He checked that the doors were locked, though many people never locked them at all. He turned down the thermostat to save on the heating bill, and turned off every light the kids had left on. Close the door, he would say, we're not heating the whole neighborhood.
scenes.query: 1950s man turning off lamp living room
scenes.caption: WE'RE NOT HEATING THE NEIGHBORHOOD

scenes.text: Saturday was for the house. Dad mowed the lawn with a push mower or a new gas-powered rotary mower. He washed the car in the driveway, with a bucket and a hose. He cleaned the gutters, painted the fence, and fixed whatever had broken during the week. The kids were expected to help, whether they wanted to or not.
scenes.caption: SATURDAY CHORES

scenes.text: Saturday was also the day for errands. The hardware store, the barber shop and the gas station, where an attendant pumped the gas, cleaned the windshield and checked the oil. Many fathers took one of the kids along. Those Saturday errands, just the two of them in the front seat, are some of the most treasured memories people have of their dads.
scenes.caption: JUST THE TWO OF US

scenes.text: And Saturday afternoon might bring a ball game. Little League, where Dad was the coach or sat in the bleachers. Or a game on the radio or television. In nineteen sixty, baseball was America's game. Many fathers taught their sons, and sometimes their daughters, to throw, catch and keep score.
scenes.caption: PLAYING CATCH

scenes.text: Saturday night, Mom and Dad might go out. Dinner at a steakhouse, a movie, or a party at the neighbors' house. A babysitter came for fifty cents an hour. Dad put on a sport coat. Mom put on a dress and a little perfume. For a few hours, they were a couple again, not just parents.
scenes.caption: SATURDAY NIGHT

scenes.text: Every summer, there was the family vacation. Dad planned the route with a road map from the gas station, and packed the trunk like a puzzle. The family drove to the lake, the beach, the mountains or Grandma's house. Dad drove the whole way. He didn't stop unless he absolutely had to, and he always wanted to beat his time from last year.
scenes.caption: THE FAMILY VACATION

scenes.text: Sunday morning, the family went to church. Dad wore his best suit. The kids squirmed in the pew. Afterward, he shook hands with the minister and talked with the other men on the church steps. Then it was home for Sunday dinner. Pot roast or fried chicken, the best meal of the week.
scenes.caption: SUNDAY MORNING

scenes.text: Sunday afternoon was for relaxing. Dad might take a nap, watch football, or take the family for a Sunday drive in the country, for no reason at all except to look at the farms and the trees. Kids sat in the back seat. Somebody always had to go to the bathroom.
scenes.caption: THE SUNDAY DRIVE

scenes.text: Or he might fire up the grill. By nineteen sixty, the backyard barbecue was a new suburban tradition, and it was Dad's domain. Hamburgers, hot dogs and steaks, cooked over charcoal with an apron and a long fork. Neighbors drifted over. The kids ran through the sprinkler. Those were good afternoons.
scenes.caption: DAD'S DOMAIN

scenes.text: And Sunday night, he got ready for the week. He polished his shoes on a sheet of newspaper on the kitchen floor. He laid out a clean shirt. He wound the alarm clock. Then he looked in on the kids, already asleep, and went to bed himself. Six o'clock would come very soon.
scenes.caption: SUNDAY NIGHT

scenes.text: Most fathers of nineteen sixty didn't talk much about their feelings. They had grown up in the Depression, when there wasn't time for that. Many had seen terrible things in the war, and never spoke about them. Their children knew their fathers had been in the war, but often learned the details only after they died.
scenes.caption: HE NEVER SPOKE ABOUT IT

scenes.text: They showed love differently. By working long hours. By teaching you to ride a bike, change a tire or bait a hook. By sitting through every school play and recital. By slipping you five dollars when you went off on a date. By being there, every single day.
scenes.caption: THEY SHOWED IT DIFFERENTLY

scenes.text: And many of them had a gentle side that only came out at certain times. Reading the Sunday funnies to a little one on his lap. Carving the Thanksgiving turkey. Putting together a bicycle at two in the morning on Christmas Eve, swearing quietly at the instructions. Walking a daughter down the aisle, and trying very hard not to cry.
scenes.caption: HIS GENTLE SIDE

scenes.text: Many children of those fathers say they didn't fully understand them until much later. When they had their own mortgages, their own jobs and their own kids. Then, suddenly, they understood why Dad was so tired, why he worried about money, and why he worked so hard. It was all for them.
scenes.caption: IT WAS ALL FOR THEM

scenes.text: The role of fathers was starting to change, even in nineteen sixty. Television shows like Father Knows Best and The Donna Reed Show presented fathers as wise and gentle. Dr. Spock encouraged fathers to be more involved with their babies. Some fathers began changing diapers and pushing strollers, which their own fathers had never done.
scenes.caption: FATHER KNOWS BEST

scenes.text: Over the next few decades, the role of fathers would change dramatically. Today's dads are often in the delivery room, at the pediatrician and in the kitchen. But the fathers of nineteen sixty laid the foundation. They gave their children stability, security and a chance at a better life than they'd had.
scenes.caption: THEY LAID THE FOUNDATION

scenes.text: If your father was a dad in nineteen sixty, take a moment to think of him. The hat on the hook by the door. The smell of his aftershave. The sound of his car pulling into the driveway. The way he said your name. He may not have said much, but he said it every day by showing up.
scenes.caption: THINK OF HIM

scenes.text: So tell us in the comments. What do you remember most about your father? What did he do for a living, and what did he teach you? We read every comment, and we'd love to hear about him. Next time, we're telling the story of the rise and fall of Woolworth's. Thank you for spending this time with me.
scenes.caption: TELL US ABOUT YOUR FATHER
